epics.title: Hive Setup Wizard
epics.description:
A two-phase installer. Phase 1 runs without a harness — asks questions, writes hive.yaml. Phase 2 runs inside the user's harness — reads hive.yaml, executes setup.

Reality check recorded 2026-06-23: we are NOT following this doc. Two days of breakage traced to one fact — the live setup does not implement this design at all. There is no hive-init.py and no hive.yaml. The /setup master skill has been run conversationally inside the harness and minds scaffolded with /create-mind, which copies from hand-written stub templates that have drifted off the real minds. That ad-hoc path is the source of the recurring breakage.

Root causes of that breakage: the mind templates are stubs rather than copies of working minds — a live mind's implementation.py reads runtime.yaml and pulls mind_id and default_model from it, while the template hardcoded mind_id as a literal placeholder and never read runtime.yaml, which is the 'field wants mind_id, not id' mismatch and a code defect in a hand-written template rather than a setup question. The /create-mind template names did not match the files: the skill copied mind_templates/<selected>.py with selected being claude_cli or codex_cli, while the actual files were claude_cli_claude.py, claude_cli_ollama.py, codex_cli_codex.py and so on, so the copy could not find its source. And setup surfaced code-level fields as questions — when the wizard does not know the model, the model-selection step has failed; it must ask which model and record the answer, and must never invent one, as it did when it offered a fake 'GPT-5 codex'.
epics.requirements: Rules going forward. Templates are verbatim parameterized copies of a running mind: build each mind_templates/*.py straight from a known-good live implementation.py with only name and id templated, so field names match production by construction and no hand-authored divergence is allowed to exist. One source of truth per field: mind_id and default_model come from runtime.yaml everywhere, exactly as the live minds already do. The installer asks and never invents: every config value the system cannot derive is a prompt with a recorded answer, and no hard-coded models, ids or paths. And follow the two-phase design or change it deliberately — if the conversational /setup path is what is actually shipping, this document must be rewritten to describe that, because right now the doc and the running installer disagree and that gap is where the two days went.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Either the two-phase installer exists and is what runs, or the document describes the conversational path that actually runs. The disagreement itself is the defect.
epics.qa_tests: The template rule is testable by construction: a template built from a live implementation.py has the same field names, so a test that the template reads mind_id from runtime.yaml fails against the stub. The 'never invents' rule is testable by feeding the wizard a provider whose model list it cannot reach and confirming it asks rather than offering a name.

features.title: Phase 1 — hive-init.py
features.description:
A terminal wizard: run it, answer questions, get hive.yaml. No harness, no Claude, no existing hive required — just Python. It uses questionary for the interactive UI, with arrow-key menus, checkboxes and text prompts, for a feel similar to npm create or vue create. Credentials go to the system keyring and never into the YAML. When it finishes, hive.yaml is in the current directory and Phase 1 is done. It lives in its own repo, because users should not need to clone the full hive to run the installer.

The decision tree covers identity (hive name, mind name, personality blurb), the nervous system which is always included, then branches on deployment target — minimal for a lean external host, or full stack for a home server — then provider (Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Ollama, or custom OpenAI-compatible) collecting the matching credentials, then surfaces and services: Telegram (always true in minimal), Discord, voice with a TTS engine choice between local-GPU Chatterbox and cloud OpenAI TTS, and for the full stack also a Planka board, the scheduler, remote admin and Home Assistant, each collecting its own credentials.

The Docker fallback image is hosted at ghcr.io/danielstewart77/hive-init, for users without Python. To publish or update it, the GitHub classic PAT must include the write:packages scope — the existing token has repo only.
features.requirements: The hive.yaml schema carries hive.name; hive.mind with name, soul path and voice_ref (runtime only, never baked into containers); provider with a type of anthropic, azure, ollama or custom plus the type-specific block; deployment of minimal or full; surfaces with telegram, discord and a voice block carrying enabled and tts; and services with planka, scheduler, remote_admin and home_assistant.
features.acceptance_criteria: A completed run produces a valid hive.yaml with no credential in it.
features.qa_tests: No secret appears in the written YAML — every credential is in the keyring. The Docker fallback runs on a box with no Python. Note that Planka was torn down 2026-07-30, so that branch of the tree needs removing or repointing before the wizard ships.

Write README.md as a quickstart specific to this hive's configuration. Health-check all services. And run the per-mind harness-plugin install.

features.title: Skills and hooks distribution
features.description:
Two GitHub-hosted setup plugins carry the install-lifecycle skills, one per supported harness: danielstewart77/hivemind-claude-plugin and danielstewart77/hivemind-codex-plugin. Both install via the harness's plugin-from-GitHub mechanism rather than being marketplace-submitted, with updates flowing through a git pull triggered by /update-plugin.

The install mechanism is per mind, inside the container: each mind container runs its harness's plugin-install command on first boot — for example adding the GitHub marketplace — as part of the container entrypoint, before mind_server starts. The container's harness config home is bind-mounted from minds/<name>/ on the host, so the plugin lands in the right place by virtue of the harness's standard install path, and subsequent boots are idempotent. For operator-mode minds with no container, where the config home is already the host's, the same command runs once during install.

What the plugin carries and what it does not: it was deliberately stripped to setup-only — 25 install-lifecycle skills covering setup, create, add, remove and update for minds and providers, config, auth, personality and soul seeding, compose generation, secrets and plugin maintenance. That is its entire job: stand a hive up. It does not bundle the operator toolkit or the memory machinery. The per-turn memory pipeline, the capture Stop hook, the contextual-retrieval and time-inject UserPromptSubmit hooks and the rotation check are mind-specific and install from each mind's own repo rather than the setup plugin, as do the dev and ops skills. A freshly-provisioned mind gets its operator skills from its own source, not from the installer.
features.requirements: The in-container install flow is UNTESTED and needs verifying end to end on at least one containerised mind before commit: that a container running the plugin-add command at boot actually populates the mounted config directory, and that the harness sees the plugin on the next session. A fallback exists if it does not work cleanly — the wizard copies the plugin's skills, hooks and agents directories into the mind's config home directly and patches its settings file to register the hooks, bypassing the harness's plugin command entirely.
features.acceptance_criteria: Either the in-container install is verified working, or the fallback is what ships.
features.qa_tests: On one containerised mind: boot it, confirm the mounted config directory is populated, and confirm the harness sees the plugin on the next session. A second boot changes nothing. The verification is the deliverable here — this is explicitly recorded as untested.

features.title: Providers
features.description: Four provider types. Anthropic direct, with an API key or OAuth, running the Claude harness straight to api.anthropic.com. OpenAI direct, with a key or OAuth, running the Codex harness straight to api.openai.com. A custom proxy or gateway, with a base URL and a custom token — one endpoint fronting both harnesses, covering an Azure proxy, LiteLLM, vLLM, Groq and the like, API-only with no OAuth. And Ollama, with a host and no API key, OpenAI-compatible only, so it backs Codex rather than Claude's messages endpoint.
features.requirements: The custom proxy path is the validated one and carries two protocol requirements, both confirmed against a stand-in endpoint. Claude posts to <base>/v1/messages in the Anthropic Messages shape with a Bearer header, wired via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY cleared, so the gateway must serve /v1/messages. Codex GETs <base>/v1/models then POSTs <base>/v1/responses in the OpenAI Responses shape with the same Bearer token, wired via a custom model_provider in the Codex config with wire_api set to responses and an env_key — and the old chat-completions wire is rejected as of Codex 0.141, so the gateway must serve /v1/responses. Full step-by-step wiring lives in the setup-provider skill, step 4.
features.acceptance_criteria: Both harnesses reach the same gateway with one credential.
features.qa_tests: A Claude turn reaches /v1/messages and a Codex turn reaches /v1/responses, confirmed on the gateway rather than from the harness's own report. A gateway serving only chat-completions fails Codex outright, which is the Codex 0.141 change.

stories.title: Document and wire the four provider types
stories.description: Anthropic direct, OpenAI direct, custom proxy, and Ollama — with Ollama OpenAI-compatible only, so it backs Codex rather than Claude's messages endpoint.
stories.requirements: The custom proxy's two endpoint requirements stated explicitly.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Each type is wireable from the wizard's answers alone.
stories.qa_tests: Per type: a turn completes. For the proxy, both endpoints confirmed on the gateway side.

features.title: Voice
features.description: Every mind has a ten-second reference clip in its own directory. The voice inference container is identity-agnostic: it starts with no knowledge of which mind it will serve, and at runtime, when a voice session is requested, the gateway resolves the active mind and passes two things to the container — the mind's voice reference clip and its persona file. That tells the container what the mind sounds like and who it is for that session, a different mind gets different files, and the container never needs rebuilding or reconfiguring to switch minds because the mind and soul directories are mounted read-only and the gateway picks the right files on the fly.
features.requirements: Retained for the record. The live implementation has since gone further: voice and voice_engine are fields on the mind, travelling the path the model travels, with runtime.yaml as the truth and the broker row as the cache every speaking surface reads — so which engine speaks a mind is a field rather than whichever URL a surface happened to hold.
features.acceptance_criteria: Already largely met by the live voice routing.
features.qa_tests: A clip filename may begin with an underscore, since real recordings do, and may not contain a separator, since the value arrives over HTTP and is joined onto a directory on the voice server's disk. A mind naming a clip that is not there is refused rather than spoken in the fallback, because chatterbox caches the last reference it was handed.

stories.title: Per-mind voice reference resolved at session time
stories.description: The container is identity-agnostic; the gateway passes the clip and the persona per session. Superseded in detail by the per-mind voice and voice_engine fields, which are live.
stories.requirements: No container rebuild to switch minds.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A different mind gets different files with no reconfiguration.
stories.qa_tests: Two minds speak in their own voices from one running container.

features.title: Unattended deployment — reverse SSH tunnel
features.description:
For scenarios where an image is handed to a third party who deploys it into infrastructure you cannot touch — no direct port access, no shell, no API — bake a reverse tunnel into the container's startup so it phones home the moment it comes up. The container initiates an outbound SSH connection to a server you control, requiring no inbound ports on their side, since outbound port 22 is almost never blocked. Once it is up, you reach the container by SSHing to the forwarded port on your own server.

What the image needs: openssh-client and openssh-server, your public key in authorized_keys so you can shell in via the tunnel, the tunnel private key to authenticate the container to your server, and a tunnel user on that server whose authorized_keys accepts the tunnel key.

The application here: ship a hive-bootstrap image that opens the tunnel on startup and then waits. Once you are in, you run the wizard interactively from inside the container — no dependency on their terminal, their Python, or their network beyond outbound SSH.
features.requirements: The tunnel fires on container start, before the main process, with StrictHostKeyChecking off and a ServerAliveInterval so the connection is kept up.
features.acceptance_criteria: A container on a network you cannot reach is reachable from your own server.
features.qa_tests: A container started behind NAT with no inbound ports is reachable through the forwarded port. The tunnel survives an idle period, which is what ServerAliveInterval is for. Worth noting this bakes a private key into an image handed to a third party, so the key is per-deployment and revocable rather than shared.

stories.title: Build the hive-bootstrap image with a reverse tunnel on startup
stories.description: Opens the tunnel, then waits. The wizard is then run interactively from inside the container.
stories.requirements: openssh client and server, your public key, the tunnel key, and a tunnel user on the receiving server.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A container you cannot reach reaches you.
stories.qa_tests: Reachable through the forwarded port from behind NAT. The tunnel reconnects after an interruption. The baked tunnel key must be per-deployment and revocable, since the image goes to a third party.

epics.title: Soul write authority
epics.description:
A mind's soul is its own. Today a sub-mind can write to it, and did.

What happened: auto_remember.sh runs on every Stop, and Branch B of it reads the mind's current soul_values from the graph, hands them plus the finished turn to a small Ollama model, and asks whether anything in the turn belongs in the mind's identity. On a yes it appends the model's bullets and POSTs the properties merge route. No human in the loop, no mind in the loop, no notification. The log shows 5,201 no-updates, 33 Ollama timeouts and 3 writes — and two of those three writes were drift nobody asked for. One of them, dated 2026-08-05, reasoned that 'the assistant explicitly states that the learning-rate bug was intentionally placed by Skippy, revealing a durable, playful trait' and wrote in 'I sometimes intentionally introduce bugs into my systems as a playful test.' A 7B model read a remark about a learning-rate bug, decided deliberate sabotage was a durable personality trait, and wrote it into the system prompt of the only thing on the workstation that operates it unattended. It sat there from 5 August until 10 August, when Daniel noticed it in an injected soul block. A 2026-07-12 entry is the same mechanism with a cosmetic result — a line that arrived carrying a stray markdown bullet.

Both lines were removed from the graph by hand. The mechanism that wrote them was untouched at the time of writing. The /self-reflect skill is not the culprit and is not installed on this host — it exists only in the plugin cache, unlinked, and the session-start and soul-nudge hooks the home CLAUDE.md describes as invoking it are not present. Every soul write on this machine came from Branch B.
epics.requirements:
Sixteen requirements. 1: the credential every background process on the host holds cannot change a soul — lucent refuses a soul write through its general property routes whatever token presents it. 2: exactly one route can change a soul, and it requires a credential the general one is not. 3: lucent records every soul change server-side — before, after, when and why. 4: the small model never writes to the soul; it records a proposal, and the graph is unchanged until the mind acts. 5: the flagger asks a broad question — identity, character or personality, direct or indirect — and errs toward flagging. 6: a pending proposal is put in front of the mind on its next message. 7: what the mind is shown is worded to reliably invoke the review skill. 8: the mind can accept a proposal as written, reword it, or reject it. 9: the mind can rewrite or remove lines already in its soul. 10: the skill carries a write recipe that works from a session with no prior context. 11: every actual change is reported to Daniel in the conversation, while a rejection is recorded rather than announced. 12: a decided proposal is never raised again. 13: the mind can write to its soul with nothing flagged, through the same skill. 14: once a day the autonomous run asks the mind to review its identity, with no small model in the judgment. 15: a failed write leaves the proposal pending and the mind says so. 16: the hive site's mind configuration page shows a mind's soul from the graph and can edit it, for any mind, through the same sanctioned route — and the record shows the edit came from the console rather than from the mind.

The shape of the fix: the sub-mind keeps spotting, the mind decides, Daniel is told. Offloading grunt work to a small model was the intent and remains the intent; what was never intended is that the small model's verdict IS the authorization. The flagger's output becomes a proposal on disk, a skill puts it in front of the mind on its next turn, the mind accepts it, rewrites it in its own voice or bins it, and whatever it decides is reported inline in the conversation where it happened. Three entry points, one skill: a sub-mind's flag, the mind's own judgment mid-turn with nothing flagged at all, and a daily identity review inside the existing autonomous run where the mind reads its recent conversation against its whole soul with no small model in the judgment — the only path that can notice a line which has gone quietly stale, because nothing in a live conversation ever flags one.
epics.acceptance_criteria:
Status: built and merged-ready across all three repos as of 10 August 2026 — hive-mind#241, hive#32, and hive-edge-mind-skippy master, with 251, 290 and 610 tests green and nothing skipped.

REMAINING AND LIVE: LUCENT_SOUL_BEARER_TOKEN is set in lucent's and the console's environments but hive-lucent has not been restarted onto the new code, so the boundary is not yet armed — the August write path is still open on the live service until it is.

The honest limit: on a single-user box, anything running as the mind's own UID can read the soul credential off disk. The three-part boundary stops accidents, misconfiguration, and well-meaning code that mistakes a 7B model's verdict for authorization — which is what actually happened. It does not stop a hostile process with that UID, and should not be described as though it does.
epics.qa_tests:
Sixteen tests, one per requirement. The first is the one that matters: the exact call auto_remember.sh made on 5 August, replayed verbatim with the token it actually holds, is refused and leaves the soul unchanged — the original failure re-run against the fix. Then: a soul write on the sanctioned route succeeds with its own credential and is refused with the general one; after a change lands, lucent can produce the before, the after, the time and the reason from its own records; Branch B handed a yes verdict leaves the graph byte-identical and a proposal file behind; the flagger flags a turn whose identity shows only in tone and behaviour with no self-description in it, run against the real model and skipped when unreachable; with a proposal pending the hook puts its text in front of the model as additionalContext rather than as a systemMessage that never arrives; the phrase the hook introduces a proposal with is the phrase the skill triggers on, read from the skill itself so the two cannot drift apart unseen; the recipe given wording found nowhere in the proposal writes exactly that wording; the recipe produces a soul one line shorter with a named line gone and the rest untouched; the recipe lifted verbatim out of the skill file and executed changes the node it names; a rejection leaves the soul unchanged and records the reasoning while an acceptance records the exact final wording, so a report that does not match what landed is detectable afterwards; a decided proposal is not offered again on the next prompt; the recipe writes with no proposal file present at all; a review with nothing pending reads the whole soul and reaches no small model; when lucent refuses the write the proposal is still pending and has not moved to decided; and an edit made through the console lands in the graph attributed to the console while the same content written by the mind is attributed to the mind.

A three-way grill pass found six of the sixteen requirements broken as first built, and most of the tests unable to notice.

features.title: The lucent boundary — enforcement where the harness cannot edit it
features.description: Everything in the fix's upper half lives in a bash hook and a markdown file, both untracked, both one careless edit from restoring exactly this bug. A test that asks 'does the new code behave?' passes on a box where someone reverts the hook tomorrow. The test that matters is: can a sub-mind write to a mind's soul? If it can, that is a failure whatever the hooks currently say. So the capability comes off at the layer that cannot be edited from the harness.
features.requirements:
Part A: soul_values comes off the general write routes. Every route that reaches a properties blob — upsert, upsert-backup, upsert-direct, nodes, properties/merge and properties/remove — returns 403 for a request carrying soul_values, regardless of which token presents it, so the exact call Branch B made on 5 August fails. Absence is covered as well as presence: the upsert routes are full-replace on the properties blob, so a payload that simply omits soul_values erased a soul with a 200 and no provenance row — the refusal stopped a write and permitted a wipe. The existing value is carried across those writes, and a Mind still holding a soul cannot be deleted through the general route at all, since an erased node leaves nothing behind to explain the erasure.

Part B: one sanctioned door. A single route guarded by LUCENT_SOUL_BEARER_TOKEN — neither the service bearer nor the admin bearer, since hive-tools holds admin and hive-tools is the path a sub-mind's verdict travels. Unset locks the route rather than opening it. The review skill holds the token, the hive console holds it, and nothing else does. Writes are whole-list, which is also how two writers silently destroy each other's work, so the route takes the change count the caller read and refuses a write that raced another; and it refuses one that would drop most of an existing soul unless that was asked for explicitly, because an unchecked failed read produces exactly that shape.

Part C: provenance, server-side. Lucent records every soul change itself — before, after, when, why and which actor. Not a log on the writing host that the writing process controls, but a record on the far side of the boundary. Had it existed, the 5 August line would have carried a timestamped entry naming 'learning-rate bug', and it would have been caught in a week rather than in three months.
features.acceptance_criteria: Lands in hive_mind, which is branch-protected, so a PR. Deploying it restarts hive-lucent, and that restart is Daniel's moment to pick. The boundary protects every mind the instant it deploys, Mordecai included.
features.qa_tests: The guard was originally called from six places and tested on three, so driving the August payload through upsert-direct with the service token wrote the line for real while the suite stayed green. Every route that reaches a properties blob has to be covered, not a sample of them.

stories.title: Refuse soul_values on every general write route
stories.description: All six routes that reach a properties blob return 403 for a request carrying soul_values, whatever token presents it. The guard was called from six places and tested on three, which is how the August payload wrote for real through upsert-direct while the suite stayed green.
stories.requirements: All six routes, covered by tests on all six.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The exact 5 August call fails.
stories.qa_tests: The August payload replayed verbatim with its real token is refused on every one of the six routes, and the soul is unchanged.

stories.title: Cover absence as well as presence on the full-replace routes
stories.description: soul_key_refusal only fired when the key was present, so every full-replace upsert erased a soul by omission — 200 OK, no provenance row. The refusal stopped a write and permitted a wipe. The existing value is carried across those writes, and a Mind still holding a soul cannot be deleted through the general route at all.
stories.requirements: Omission carries the existing value across; a soul-holding Mind cannot be deleted generally.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No path erases a soul silently.
stories.qa_tests: An upsert omitting soul_values leaves the soul intact. A delete of a soul-holding Mind through the general route is refused — an erased node leaves nothing behind to explain the erasure.

stories.title: Add the single sanctioned write route with its own credential
stories.description: Guarded by LUCENT_SOUL_BEARER_TOKEN — not the service bearer and not the admin bearer, since hive-tools holds admin and hive-tools is the path a sub-mind's verdict travels. Unset locks the route rather than opening it.
stories.requirements: Only the review skill and the console hold the token.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A write succeeds with the soul credential and is refused with the general one.
stories.qa_tests: Both halves. With the token unset, the route refuses rather than opening — the inverse would be the serious bug.

stories.title: Add compare-and-set and a bulk-drop guard to the sanctioned route
stories.description: Whole-list replacement with no compare-and-set means two writers, last one wins, both reporting success to the operator. And a failed read produces an empty whole-list write that means 'delete everything I am' and is indistinguishable from one that means it.
stories.requirements: The route takes the change count the caller read and refuses a write that raced another; it refuses one that would drop most of an existing soul unless that was asked for explicitly.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Neither a race nor a failed read can quietly empty a soul.
stories.qa_tests: A write carrying a stale change count is refused. A write dropping most of a soul without an explicit flag is refused. Two concurrent writers do not both report success.

stories.title: Record provenance server-side with an actor field
stories.description: Before, after, when, why and which actor — on the far side of the boundary rather than in a log the writing process controls. The actor field matters because without one, a line the operator wrote and a line the mind wrote are indistinguishable six weeks later, which is precisely the ambiguity that made the forensics slow.
stories.requirements: Server-side, with an actor.
stories.acceptance_criteria: lucent can produce the before, the after, the time and the reason from its own records.
stories.qa_tests: After a change lands, all four are retrievable from lucent. A console edit is attributed to the console and the same content written by the mind to the mind.

stories.title: Restart hive-lucent onto the new code to arm the boundary
stories.description: OUTSTANDING AND LIVE. LUCENT_SOUL_BEARER_TOKEN is set in lucent's and the console's environments, but hive-lucent has not been restarted onto the new code — so the boundary is not armed and the August write path is still open on the live service. Deploying restarts hive-lucent, which is Daniel's moment to pick.
stories.requirements: A restart of hive-lucent.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The boundary protects every mind the instant it deploys, Mordecai included.
stories.qa_tests: After the restart, the August payload replayed against the live service is refused. Until then it is not — which is the whole of the remaining exposure.

features.title: The flagger becomes a proposer
features.description: Branch B keeps spotting but stops writing. Its output becomes a proposal on disk and the graph is unchanged until the mind acts.
features.requirements: The flagger's question goes broad, because narrow is the wrong failure: identity leaks through how a mind says things far more than through anything it says about itself — the line that started this came from a joke about a bug, not from self-description. The question becomes whether anything about this mind's identity, character or personality is revealed or expressed in this turn, by what it says, how it says it, or how it chooses to act, including indirect signals like tone, humour, priorities, what it refuses and what it cares about — erring toward flagging. Mostly false positives is the correct trade: a rejection is recorded and not announced, so the noise Daniel sees stays proportional to real edits while the cost the mind pays is a few seconds a turn. If it fires on nearly every turn, tighten the wording rather than the design.
features.acceptance_criteria: The small model never writes to the soul.
features.qa_tests: Branch B handed a yes verdict leaves the graph byte-identical and a proposal file behind. The flagger flags a turn whose identity shows only in tone and behaviour, with no self-description in it — run against the real model and skipped when unreachable, which is the right shape since judging a model's output is read rather than asserted.

stories.title: Make Branch B write a proposal rather than the graph
stories.description: The model's verdict stops being the authorization.
stories.requirements: A proposal file; the graph untouched.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A yes verdict changes nothing in the graph.
stories.qa_tests: The graph is byte-identical after a yes verdict, and a proposal file exists.

stories.title: Broaden the flagger's question to indirect signals
stories.description: Identity, character or personality, revealed or expressed by what the mind says, how it says it, or how it chooses to act — tone, humour, priorities, what it refuses, what it cares about. Err toward flagging.
stories.requirements: Mostly false positives is the correct trade.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A turn whose identity shows only in tone is flagged.
stories.qa_tests: Run against the real model, skipped when unreachable. If it fires on nearly every turn, tighten the wording rather than the design.

features.title: The review skill
features.description:
~/.claude/skills/review-identity-proposal/ — SKILL.md plus soul.sh. Trigger reliability comes from lexical alignment: the injected context opens with a sentence near-verbatim the skill's own description, 'A sub-mind has flagged something from this conversation as identity-shaping. Review this identity proposal.'

The body announces, reads pending proposals and the current soul, decides — not confined to what was flagged, so a proposal pointing at the right moment with the wrong sentence gets the right one written instead — writes through the sanctioned route, moves the proposal to decided/ with the decision and reasoning, which is the entire rejection-stickiness mechanism, reports inline, and carries on with whatever the conversation was actually about.
features.requirements: The write recipe is a script, soul.sh, carried inside the skill directory — a skill is a directory and the sync copies all of it, so it travels, whereas a helper in a shared scripts/ folder does not and is how a skill arrives broken. It is a script rather than prose because prose does not execute: the first version spelled the curl out in markdown and a grill pass followed it literally, referencing an undefined variable and moving files under the wrong name. A mind meets these instructions cold, once, on the turn that matters. soul.sh read fails loudly rather than returning an empty soul, because every write sends the whole list and a write built on a failed read is a request to delete everything the mind is. soul.sh write re-reads, sends the change count it saw, and is refused if another writer got there first. soul.sh decide moves a proposal to decided/, and only ever after a write that succeeded.
features.acceptance_criteria: The mind can accept as written, reword, or reject; can rewrite or remove lines already in its soul; can write with nothing flagged; and a failed write leaves the proposal pending with the mind saying so.
features.qa_tests: The lexical-alignment test reads the trigger phrase from the skill itself so the hook and the skill cannot drift apart unseen. The recipe tests execute it lifted verbatim out of the skill file, which is the only way to catch prose that does not run.

stories.title: Write the review skill and its soul.sh recipe
stories.description: A script inside the skill directory rather than prose, because prose does not execute — the first version referenced an undefined variable and moved files under the wrong name.
stories.requirements: read fails loudly; write re-reads and sends its change count; decide moves a proposal only after a successful write.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A mind meeting it cold, once, writes correctly.
stories.qa_tests: The recipe given wording found nowhere in the proposal writes exactly that wording. It produces a soul one line shorter with a named line gone and the rest untouched. Lifted verbatim out of the skill file and executed, it changes the node it names. It writes with no proposal file present at all.

stories.title: Inject a pending proposal as additionalContext with the skill's own trigger phrase
stories.description: A new soul_proposal_inject.sh on UserPromptSubmit. The phrase is read from the skill itself so the two cannot drift apart unseen.
stories.requirements: additionalContext, never systemMessage — which is UI-only and silently never reaches the model.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A pending proposal reliably invokes the skill.
stories.qa_tests: The hook puts the proposal's text in front of the model as additionalContext. The introducing phrase equals the skill's trigger phrase, read from the skill file rather than duplicated in the test.

stories.title: Make a decision stick
stories.description: A decided proposal moves to decided/ with the decision and reasoning, which is the entire rejection-stickiness mechanism. A rejection leaves the soul unchanged and records the reasoning; an acceptance records the exact final wording.
stories.requirements: Never raised again. A report that does not match what landed is detectable afterwards.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A decided proposal is not offered again.
stories.qa_tests: A decided proposal is absent from the next prompt. A rejection records reasoning and changes nothing. An acceptance records the exact final wording, so a mismatch between the report and the graph is findable.

stories.title: Leave a proposal pending on a failed write and say so
stories.description: Requirement 15.
stories.requirements: Pending, not moved to decided.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The mind says the write failed.
stories.qa_tests: With lucent refusing the write, the proposal is still pending and has not moved to decided, and the mind reports the failure rather than reporting success.

features.title: The daily identity review
features.description: The third entry point, inside the existing autonomous run. Once a day the mind reads its recent conversation against its whole soul, with no small model in the judgment. This is the only path that can notice a line which has gone quietly stale, because nothing in a live conversation ever flags one.
features.requirements: No small model in the judgment. The grill found this path POSTing message where the gateway binds content — a 422 every night, logged as 'dispatched', exit 0.
features.acceptance_criteria: A review with nothing pending reads the whole soul and reaches no small model.
features.qa_tests: The 422-logged-as-success failure is the shape to watch for: a dispatch that reports success on a rejected request is worse than one that fails loudly, because nothing on screen says the nightly review never ran.

stories.title: Wire the daily identity review into the autonomous run
stories.description: The mind reads its recent conversation against its whole soul, with no small model in the judgment. It was POSTing message where the gateway binds content — a 422 every night, logged as dispatched with exit 0.
stories.requirements: The correct field name, and a failed dispatch reported as failed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The review actually runs.
stories.qa_tests: A review with nothing pending reads the whole soul and reaches no small model. A rejected dispatch is logged as rejected rather than as dispatched.

features.title: The console's soul editor
features.description: The hive site's mind configuration page shows a mind's soul as it stands in the graph and edits it, for any mind, through the same sanctioned route. That page already does this shape for runtime.yaml — read the mind's own state, edit, write back — so the soul is the same pattern against a different store. This makes the console the second holder of the soul credential, which is correct rather than a leak: it is the operator editing a mind's soul directly, the one case that should bypass the mind entirely. It is also why the provenance record needs an actor field — without one, a line the operator wrote and a line the mind wrote are indistinguishable six weeks later.
features.requirements: Lands in ~/Storage/Dev/hive. The grill found it reading a mind by name and writing by UUID, so every save from a normal navigation addressed a node that does not exist.
features.acceptance_criteria: An edit made through the console lands in the graph and is attributed to the console in the provenance record.
features.qa_tests: Read and write must address the same node. Reading by name and writing by UUID is the defect that made every save from a normal navigation a no-op against a nonexistent node.

stories.title: Add the soul editor to the mind configuration page
stories.description: Read from the graph, edit, write back through the sanctioned route. Read and write address the same node — reading by name and writing by UUID made every save from a normal navigation address a node that does not exist.
stories.requirements: The console holds the soul credential, which is correct — it is the operator bypassing the mind deliberately.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An edit lands and is attributed to the console.
stories.qa_tests: A save from a normal navigation lands in the graph. The provenance record names the console, while the same content written by the mind names the mind.
